text: The two empty cases are told apart as git does, by the actual tree state after the requested staging mode, not by the flag: a genuinely clean tree with an empty index gives 'nothing to commit, working tree clean' (e.g. mint commit -A on a pristine tree); changes that the chosen mode staged none of give a guide naming the modes that would help, e.g. bare mint commit with unstaged changes: 'no changes staged — use -a/--all, -A/--add-all, or git add'.
why: Follows the familiar git expectation rather than a bare error (review-002 F7).

text: mint commit -a when the only changes are untracked (so tracked-only -a staged nothing) points specifically at -A/--add-all, e.g. 'no tracked changes to stage — use -A/--add-all to include untracked files'.
why: Names the mode that would include them.

text: What is commit's default message format and prompt?
The default output is Conventional Commits 1.0.0: a type(scope): description subject line, imperative and concise, with an optional blank line and wrapped body for the why.
why: The user's own repos already use conventional commits (discussion(...), chore(...), docs(...)); release's TL;DR + emoji-headed format is wrong for a commit.

text: The AI infers the type (feat/fix/chore/docs/…) from the diff.
why: Central to the format and reliably inferable.

text: Scope is off by default; re-enabling or guiding scope is a prompt/config affordance if ever wanted.
why: Scope conventions are project-specific and the AI guesses them inconsistently: better omitted than wrong.

text: Two-knob override, mirroring release: a commit-specific context-inject knob and a full prompt-override knob, under the same 'mint owns the prompt; ai_command is transport' model.
why: Consistency with release's settled prompt model.

text: commit does not use release's commit_prefix (🌿): commit messages carry no mint branding in their text; commit_prefix stays release-only (release commit + tag subject).
why: A conventional-commit message is plain type(scope): …, and forcing a 🌿 onto every commit is undesirable (reviewer F7).

text: What does commit do when there is no AI message: --no-ai, AI generation failure, or a diff over max_diff_lines?
--no-ai behaves like plain git commit: drop to $EDITOR with an empty/template message for the user to write; no AI, no synthetic stub.
why: The natural fallback for a commit verb, unlike release, whose --no-ai builds a commit-subject-list body (reviewer F4).

cites.section: The `$EDITOR` fallback — one degradation path for all "no AI message" cases

text: If the AI errors or returns nothing usable after the engine's one retry, commit falls back to the same $EDITOR path rather than aborting.
why: Low-stakes and friendly: the user is at the terminal anyway.

cites.section: The `$EDITOR` fallback — one degradation path for all "no AI message" cases

text: A diff over max_diff_lines does not abort commit: it falls back to the $EDITOR path with a clear note ('diff too large to summarise — opening editor'); diff_exclude applies first, so excluded noise does not push a diff over the limit.
why: Release's notes-failure model is too harsh for a routine large commit; one consistent degradation path serves all three no-AI-message cases (reviewer F5).

cites.section: The `$EDITOR` fallback — one degradation path for all "no AI message" cases

text: max_diff_lines is evaluated at L1, after diff_exclude filtering and before any L2 call; an over-limit diff short-circuits L2 entirely as a generate-skip (like --no-ai), not a generate-failure, and routes straight to the $EDITOR fallback. The line-counting mechanics are the shared engine's; only commit's fall-back-rather-than-abort branch is commit-specific.
why: Pins the detection ordering so the oversized case is treated like a deliberate skip.

cites.section: The `$EDITOR` fallback — one degradation path for all "no AI message" cases

text: If a regeneration (r at the gate) fails after its one retry, it is treated as any other AI failure and routes to the $EDITOR fallback; there is no special 're-show the prior message' path. Under -y/non-TTY this is moot, r being interactive-only.
why: One consistent rule: any failed AI generation lands at the editor (F6).

text: How does the $EDITOR fallback reconcile with deferred staging, the review gate, and the -y/non-TTY posture?

The $EDITOR fallback requires a TTY: when a fallback fires under -y or non-TTY stdin (e.g. mint commit -Apy --no-ai, or -Apy when the AI fails or the diff is oversized), mint fails loud ('no AI message and no interactive editor available'); it never hangs and never commits an empty message.
why: Extends the gate's forbidden-combo philosophy (unattended + needs-human → fail loud) to the editor path; an unattended run with no message source is contradictory (F1).

cites.section: Decision — F1: the `$EDITOR` fallback requires a TTY

text: There is no -m/--message escape: anyone needing an unattended run with their own message uses plain git commit.
why: Kept minimal: mint commit is for minted messages.

cites.section: Decision — F1: the `$EDITOR` fallback requires a TTY

text: Every editor commit opens (the fallback and the gate's e) is resolved by git's own order: GIT_EDITOR, core.editor, $VISUAL, $EDITOR, then git's built-in default, so it opens whatever git commit would; an unset $EDITOR is not by itself an error on a TTY. mint opens the editor itself rather than delegating to git commit.
why: Staging must be deferred until the save-as-accept event, so mint cannot hand the commit to git commit.

text: When no editor in the chain resolves to a launchable program on the fallback path (no message yet), mint fails loud, as in the no-TTY/-y case.
why: There is no message to fall back to.

text: When no editor resolves on the gate's e action (a message already exists), mint degrades gracefully: it warns that the editor could not be launched and re-renders the Continue? gate with the unedited message preserved, treating e as a no-op.
why: e is a refinement step that can never produce an empty commit.

text: On the fallback path the editor replaces the Continue? gate, git-like: the gate governs the AI-generated message only; a non-empty save is accept, quit or an empty save is abort.
why: Reconciles '--no-ai behaves like plain git commit' with 'gate ON by default': the gate is AI-path-only (F3).

cites.section: Decision — F2/F3/F4: the editor save *is* the accept event

text: Staging applies on save: the editor opens against the real (unstaged) state, and only on a non-empty save does mint apply -a/-A staging, then commit; -p push then runs as normal, so mint commit -Ap --no-ai stages, commits and pushes.
why: The same stage-on-accept rule, where save is the accept; a non-empty save is a full accept, so mutate-nothing-until-accept holds (F2).

cites.section: Decision — F2/F3/F4: the editor save *is* the accept event

text: An empty or aborted editor is a true no-op: no staging, no commit, no push (even with -p).
why: Nothing was mutated, so there is nothing to clean up, consistent with the no-destructive-cleanup invariant (F4).

cites.section: Decision — F2/F3/F4: the editor save *is* the accept event

text: Does commit review the message before it lands, and how do the Continue? gate's choices map for commit?
commit reuses the cli-presentation Continue? gate rendering (y/n/e/r, Enter ⇒ accept).
why: Consistency with release and the presentation model.

cites.section: Decision — reuse the `Continue?` gate, ON by default

text: The gate is ON by default: interactive runs show the message and Continue?; -y skips it (auto-accept); the shared forbidden-combo rule applies (non-TTY stdin without -y fails loud); the frequent one-liner stays fast via -y (mint commit -Apy).
why: Seeing the minted message before it sticks is the point (F10).
rules_out: Gate OFF by default (commit immediately, review opt-in): faster for the frequent case, but commits messages unseen — the pain the gate exists to kill; -y already covers the unattended case

cites.section: Decision — reuse the `Continue?` gate, ON by default

text: y / accept stages (if -a/-A), then commits, then pushes if -p.
why: Staging is deferred to accept.

cites.section: Decision — reuse the `Continue?` gate, ON by default

text: n / abort does nothing: no auto-unwind is needed, since nothing has been mutated yet; abort is a true no-op back to the pre-mint state.
why: Commit's abort has nothing to roll back, unlike release's (F3).

cites.section: Decision — reuse the `Continue?` gate, ON by default

text: e / edit opens the resolved editor pre-filled with the current message; on save it returns to the Continue? gate with the edited message, used verbatim with no AI reprocessing (it is not save-as-accept; only the fallback editor is). From there the user may y, n, e or r again. An empty save under e discards the edit and re-renders the gate with the prior message preserved.
why: Follows the cli-presentation seam's loop-back contract; e is a refinement step, never a message source, so it can never produce an empty commit.

cites.section: Decision — reuse the `Continue?` gate, ON by default

text: r / regenerate with context is the context-injection affordance of the original shell function: mint prompts for one free-text line through the Presenter's line-read (Enter submits), injects it as one-time context into the regeneration prompt without persisting it, and an empty line re-rolls with no injected context; regeneration runs the engine's normal one retry.
why: Carries the shell function's context injection into the gate.

text: How does commit's auto-push behave, and what happens when the push fails?
Push is opt-in via -p/--push, flag-only with no config default; without -p mint never pushes.
why: The user: 'we never push without the -p flag'; the target invocation mint commit -Ap implies a flag.

text: A failed push (rejected, remote moved, no upstream, network) keeps the commit, warns clearly with the fix (re-run the push), and does not unwind: push is a best-effort final step, not an atomic point-of-no-return.
why: A push is a trivially repeatable manual fix, whereas unwinding the commit is messy and risky: resetting or unstaging could clobber files the user had staged before running mint commit (F6/F11).

text: Upstream handling defers to git: mint commit -p runs a normal git push (current branch to its configured upstream); no upstream set is git's own failure, surfaced by the warn rule; mint adds no special upstream logic.
why: Keeps commit thin and git-faithful.

text: mint does not classify push-failure causes: on any push failure it emits one generic warn (the commit is in place; re-run the push to retry) with git's own stderr passed through verbatim beneath it; the 'set an upstream and push' line is illustrative of git's pass-through, not a mint-authored per-cause message.
why: One rule for all causes keeps git's specific hint visible.

text: After accept mint never unwinds a completed commit: it never unstages, resets or rewrites, and has no destructive cleanup path at all; failures either left nothing behind (pre-accept) or leave a clean forward-only commit the user can act on (post-accept). This is the deliberate opposite of mint release's auto-unwind model.
why: A local commit verb must never risk the user's working or staged state.

text: Which preflight gates does commit run, given release's strict set (clean tree, release branch, remote in sync, tag free, gh auth)?

commit's preflight runs only two checks: a git repo is present, anchored at the repo root (same resolution as release), and there is something to commit after the requested staging (empty fails loud).
why: A commit is a frequent, low-stakes, local act; most of release's gates are actively wrong for it (F2/F9).

text: The clean-working-tree gate is dropped for commit.
why: Commit exists to operate on a dirty tree; the release gate is the direct opposite of its purpose (resolves F2).

text: The on-release-branch gate is dropped for commit.
why: Commits legitimately happen on feature branches all day.

text: The remote-in-sync (behind/diverged) gate is dropped for commit.
why: You commit while behind origin constantly; blocking that would be absurd (resolves F9).

text: There is no pre-push gate even with -p: mint does not gate the commit on push-ability or precheck remote sync; it attempts the push and reports failure.
why: Consistent with the auto-push decision.

text: Where does input enrichment live in the notes engine?

Notes generation splits into git-aware context assembly (the `last_tag..HEAD` diff, `diff_exclude` filtering, the `max_diff_lines` guard and the Change Map preamble) and a content-agnostic AI transport (prompt plus content plus `ai_command` in, validated body out, knowing nothing of git, diffs or tags).
why: Mirrors the engine's other seams and keeps the transport trivially testable with a string and a fake `ai_command`.

cites.section: Decision — adopt a directory-rollup "Change Map", structural novelty weighted above magnitude

text: Structural novelty (new, removed and renamed paths, especially new directories or packages) is the Change Map's primary signal, weighted above magnitude in both its ordering and how the prompt tells the AI to read it.
why: A new subsystem is a headline even at modest line count while a large refactor may not be; a refactor and a new feature can have identical post-exclude churn, and new structure captures the headline axis line-count cannot. It is the strongest language-agnostic headline signal.

text: How does mint handle degenerate releases: an empty diff, a release whose every changed file falls under `diff_exclude`, or pure churn with nothing notable?

text: The notes open with a one-sentence headline above the first section that sums up the release's main body of work; beneath it the categorised sections list every notable change as they would without it, the main feature's pieces included, so headline and sections overlap by design — summary, then detail.
why: In the common release the main feature is many bullets, not one, so the headline cannot be a lifted bullet; it has to be a summary, and a summary overlaps its detail. Where the main work is a single bullet the overlap costs one repeated line.
rules_out: Moving the headlined change out of its category
A headed highlight section: the decided shape is a plain sentence above the first section
alternatives: A: headline line above the sections, the headlined change moved out of its category
C: the headline as its own emoji section (e.g. a Highlight section with one bullet)
evidence: The user's hand-written switchboard v0.2.0 notes open with a plain headline sentence

text: The headline does not relieve the sections: the prompt says so, so the model does not thin them because the top line already summed them up.
why: Today's combine wording could otherwise pull the model into folding the main feature into one bullet restating the headline.

text: The combine rule stands as worded ('Combine closely-related changes into a single bullet'): closely related means the small tweaks of one change, such as three commits fixing one gate, never a feature's separate capabilities — each piece a user can use or meet on its own gets its own bullet. Only evidence on real releases of the model collapsing a large feature into one bullet would reopen its wording.
why: Each piece a user meets is a notable change in its own right, and mint 0.0.6 kept mint setup's pieces apart under today's wording; where the model still folds a feature into one bullet, the cost is one repeated line.
evidence: The audit found the model never collapsed a large feature into a single bullet; it over-splits

text: The headline is one sentence held to the bullets' altitude — terse, plain language, the change and what it gives its user — never a synthesis of everything in the release and never a narrative thread tying the changes together.
why: A narrative 'what is this release about' is what grew into the essay-length TL;DR that 886c6100 cut.

text: The headline leads with what the release gives its user — what users can now do, or no longer suffer, in the terms they meet it, never in files, formats or internals — not the scope of the work: no scale or praise words ('major', 'overhaul', 'powerful') and no inventory of the work's pieces; the sections carry the scale.
why: Asked to convey scale, the model writes an inventory with an adjective on the front — the TL;DR compressed into one sentence plus marketing inflation; the list beneath shows how much work it took better than 'major'.

text: The main body of work can be any kind of change — a feature, a rework, a fix or a large epic — and the headline names it whatever section its pieces sit in.
why: A release's main thing is not always an addition.

text: The headline is plain text — no bold, no emoji, no label such as 'Highlights:' or 'TL;DR:' — and is the body's first line, followed by one blank line and then the first section.
why: Position and the blank line already set it apart, and in a raw CHANGELOG.md the asterisks are noise.

text: The headline is the only thing that may appear above the first section: no summary paragraph, no TL;DR, no label, no other preamble; the default prompt's 'start directly with the first section header' gives way to this headline-or-first-section rule.
why: The no-preamble rule must allow exactly the one headline line while still forbidding the paragraph that grew into the essay.

text: The notes carry no wrapper, markers or machine-parseable labels, and no commentary or sign-off; the one body without sections is the maintenance line for a release with nothing users meet.
why: The default prompt asks for the body and nothing else.

text: Bullets are unchanged: each is one line and one sentence, the change in plain language with its user-facing effect after an em dash where that helps — no second sentence, bold lead-in, sub-bullets, implementation detail or rationale for how it was built — and the shipped prompt's three altitude examples stay as they are.
why: The one-line discipline from 886c6100 is kept; the headline is held to the same altitude.

text: One bullet per notable change, never one per file, hunk or commit; version bumps and other bookkeeping churn are ignored; most releases are a handful of bullets, and the notes are not padded.
why: Carried unchanged from the shipped prompt.

text: Deprecated and Security stay opportunistic: an item goes in them only on an explicit marker in the diff (a @deprecated annotation, or an obvious auth, cryptography, input-validation or CVE-bump surface), never inferred.
why: Carried unchanged from the shipped prompt.

text: A main body of work gets a headline: one feature, rework or fix that anyone asked 'what is this release?' would name. The test, run against the notes' own bullets: most of the notable changes serve it, or it alone clearly outweighs all the other changes put together; the largest of several separate changes is not a main body of work.
why: E1's tuning showed the call flipping on and off until v3's countable test made it repeatable: headline presence agreed between repeats on all 26 held-out releases.

cites.section: No Clear Headline > Decision > 2026-10-22 — revised (two bodies and the main-body test)

text: A release with two bodies of work of equal weight names both in its one headline sentence — at most two, still one sentence, still led by the benefit; more than two co-equal bodies is not designed for, the one-sentence limit stands and the model handles the case as best it can.
why: A headline naming one of two equal halves misrepresents the release, and omitting it costs the lead on the largest releases; three co-equal features are rare enough at mint's cadence not to design for.
alternatives: Pick the bigger one; the other lives only in the sections
Omit the headline whenever no single thing dominates

text: Each of two co-equal bodies takes the main-body test with the other set aside; testing the pair together also fits but is the looser reading at the margin.
why: Testing each body against the other would leave the two-body rule dead; the per-body test keeps the test the grab-bag call already uses and leans to omission where the readings differ.

cites.section: No Clear Headline > Decision > 2026-10-22 — revised (two bodies and the main-body test)

text: A headline names a second subject only when it is a co-equal body of work: never two pieces of one body, and never a main body plus a lesser piece.
why: E1's new-v3 barred a lesser second subject only where 'And' joins it; the specification bars any second subject that is not a co-equal body.

text: No headline where one bullet already states the whole release and nothing else stands beside it; where the main work is spread over several bullets none naming the whole, the headline stays even when the notes hold nothing else, and a main feature written as a single bullet beside unrelated changes keeps its headline too. The test is whether a single bullet states the whole release, not a bullet count.
why: The headline's job is to state the whole and stand it apart; it is dropped only where a bullet already does both. The audit found releases made only of their main work are where it is split into the most pieces, none naming it, so there the headline is the only line saying what the release is.
rules_out: Dropping the headline wherever the notes hold nothing but the main thing
A bullet-count test
alternatives: Consistency: every release opening the same way, even when the top line repeats the only change

text: A grab-bag release — small unrelated changes, no main body of work, however large the largest of them — carries no headline; its notes start with the first section.
why: With no main body of work there is nothing to sum up, and a theme stitched across unrelated changes is the invented narrative the format removed.
evidence: The audit's grab-bag is dex-engine v0.2.9; the user's hand-written switchboard v0.2.4 grab-bag opens with no headline
E1's v3 held the grab-bag headline out on both tuning repeats

text: When in doubt, leave it out: the AI writes a headline only when one body of work (or two co-equal ones) clearly stands out, and otherwise starts with the first section. Accepted cost: some releases that deserved a headline go without one. On an attended run the review gate's existing correctives remain: e to edit, r to regenerate with a one-time nudge.
why: A missing headline costs no more than today's notes; a wrong one misstates the release in its most-read line, and on an unattended run (mint release -y, as agent sessions run it) nobody reads the notes before they ship.
evidence: E1: no wrong-subject or unexpected headline in 52 bodies; every miss an omission or half of a two-body release

text: Only the AI-written body, through the notes prompt, can carry a headline; mint and its AI add none to the selector's other bodies — the first release's fixed 'Initial release.' body, the maintenance stub for an empty post-exclusion diff, the commit-subject body under --no-ai or when the AI fails under on_notes_failure = fallback, a --notes-file body, and the body the operator chooses at the notes floor after the AI fails on an attended run (the commit subjects, or notes written in the editor). A body the operator writes carries one only if the operator writes it.
why: These bodies never see the headline rules, and mint writing a line into them would be the injection the byte-identical invariant forbids.

cites.section: No Clear Headline > Decision > 2026-10-22 — revised (bodies the notes prompt never writes)

text: The AI picks the headline by what the release changes for its user, read from the diff; a new folder or a large file is not, of itself, the release's main thing, and the Change Map does not pick the headline.
why: The structural signal cannot identify a release's main thing: it is near-blind where code is nested (it reads only a path's first segment) and flags novelty rather than user weight where it fires, while a headline turns any misread from a reordered list into a misstatement in the most-read line.

text: The AI's inputs are unchanged: every notes call carries the resolved instructions, the Change Map and the closing reminder, with the post-exclusion diff, one part's slice or, for the merge, every part's notes; nothing is added, commit history stays out, and the diff stays the only source of truth for what changed. The known limit — the building session knows the headline better than the diff — is left to a supplied headline and not closed here.
why: Feeding commit history to the AI was dropped in release-notes-quality and is not reopened.
rules_out: Feeding commit history to the AI

text: Everything mint adds to every notes call — the closing reminder, the chunk and piece framings, the merge framing — stays format-neutral; every headline rule, and every rule of the format, lives in the default prompt alone.
why: The reminder's job — the body is the notes, nothing else — is the same on every repo, and the headline belongs to one format; one neutral rule that points back at the governing format serves both.
rules_out: mint's format leaking into override repos' calls
Two reminders kept in step by hand
alternatives: A: the reminder names the headline (E1's tested wording)
B: the reminder switches by prompt source

cites.section: Prompt Overrides And Reminder > Options Considered

text: The closing reminder becomes: 'Now output ONLY the release notes themselves, in the format above, exactly as they should be published: no preamble, no commentary, no explanation, no code fences, nothing before or after the notes.' — 'the format above' meaning whichever instructions govern, on the default prompt a format that opens with the headline. Only evidence that the model keeps a headline when the last thing it reads names one would reopen it.
why: It keeps the reminder's single job, the hardening against models narrating before the notes, while the format stays with the instructions; E1's headline-naming wording would tell an override repo's model to put a headline above sections its format may not have.

text: Repos on the default prompt, with or without [release].context (appended under its labelled header), get the headline and every rule of the format; a full [release].prompt override is the operator's format, gets no headline unless the operator's prompt asks for one, and only mint's shared wording reaches its calls.
why: The default prompt is where the format lives, and nothing mint adds to an override's calls asks for a headline.

text: Part calls write no headline; the merge call alone writes it, judging the whole release from every part's notes and the whole-release Change Map.
why: A part sees one slice and cannot know whether it is the release's main work or a footnote, and the merge is the only call that sees the whole; parts writing their own would leave the merge four competing leads and a failed merge's saved file four headlines stacked.
alternatives: B: parts write headlines and the merge chooses among them

text: The chunk and piece framings ask, in format-neutral terms, that a part leave out anything that sums up the release as a whole, because the merge writes that: on the default prompt the headline, and under an override whose format has no such line, nothing.
why: mint's shared wording stays format-neutral.

text: A part whose slice holds nothing the notes would list returns one line saying so — a statement about its part, never about the release — and the part framing says this in format-neutral terms.
why: Only the merge sees the whole release; a part that returns nothing fails the transport and the run, and the release's maintenance line is itself a summary of the whole release a part must leave out.

text: The merge leaves the parts' nothing-to-list lines out, and where every part returned one it writes what the governing format gives a release with nothing to list — on the default prompt the maintenance line; the merge framing says this in format-neutral terms.
why: Only the merge can say the release has nothing for its users.

text: Under a full [release].prompt override whose format gives no body for a release with nothing to list, the merge framing supplies no fallback of its own: the merge writes what it can from that format, and an empty body it returns fails the call as any empty body does.
why: The override is the operator's format, and a fallback line would carry the maintenance-line rule into mint's shared wording, which stays format-neutral.

text: The saved part-notes file's rule stands (each finished part's notes byte for byte, in chunk order, a blank line between parts, a **Notes missing:** line on top when any slice has none); it carries no headline and holds the parts' sections plus any part's nothing-to-list line, which the operator removes while tidying, as with the **Notes missing:** line.
why: This feature changes what the part calls return, not the file's rule.

text: The README's Saved part notes paragraph is the one text that tells the operator to delete the marker line; the release floor's next move tells the operator to tidy the saved notes, 'filling in any files its marker lists' (internal/engine/notesfloor.go:69), and no next move tells the operator to delete the marker line (internal/engine/regenerate_batch.go:259 does not mention it). --notes-file refuses an empty file (README.md:324).
how: Searched the README; the next moves measured against the tree, as the corrigendum of 2026-10-23 records.

text: mint's guidance on releasing a saved file — the README's Saved part notes paragraph — tells the operator to delete the parts' nothing-to-list lines as well as the marker; the next moves mint prints when it stops, which tell the operator to tidy the saved notes, stay as they are.
why: A checklist that leaves the lines out makes them read as content to keep, and an unattended agent works from what mint tells it; 'as well as the marker' fits only the README paragraph, the one text that tells the operator to delete the marker line.

text: Where every part's notes in a saved file are the nothing-to-list line, the guidance tells the operator to release the maintenance line in their place rather than an empty file.
why: The operator tidying the file stands in for the merge that failed, a release with nothing users meet gets the maintenance line, and --notes-file refuses an empty file, so deleting the lines alone leads nowhere.

text: A release shipped from the saved part-notes file, by --notes-file or picked up with e, carries a headline only if the operator writes one while tidying.
why: It is the doubt rule on a path where no call saw the whole.

text: Every regenerate of chunked notes goes through the merge — r re-runs only the merge, and a merge re-run from saved part notes does too — so the headline and any one-time nudge stay with the call that writes the headline.
why: The merge is the call that writes the headline.

text: This feature designs no route for a headline supplied by an operator or an outer agent; the headline, one plain sentence above the first section, is the slot any later route fills, and which route to take — a steer handed to mint's AI, a finished --notes-file body, or an operator-supplied line placed above the AI's body — is the agent-authored release notes item's call.
why: The brief is not to foreclose; the user favoured the steer, doubted it is easy, and placed it outside this work, which the roadmap item already covers. The review gate's r nudge is the existing steer mechanism such a route would reuse.

cites.section: Room For A Supplied Headline > Decision
Room For A Supplied Headline > Journey

text: The byte-identical rule is read as protecting what the AI or the operator wrote from mint's own edits and additions: mint never parses, reformats or adds to a notes body and never writes or edits a headline of its own, and nothing here rules out an operator-supplied line placed above the AI's body.
why: The rule exists so mint never rewrites or brands what someone wrote; a line the operator hands over is the operator's content, as a --notes-file body is. The literal reading ('a headline has to come from the AI's output') foreclosed one route on an invariant that does not reach it.

cites.section: Room For A Supplied Headline > Decision
Room For A Supplied Headline > Journey

text: mint titles every provider release with the bare tag: the forward release and both regenerate paths pass the tag as the title.
how: Searched the engine's release and regenerate sources.
command: rg -n 'CreateRelease\(ctx, tag, tag' internal/engine/release.go; rg -n 'DispatchRelease\(' internal/engine/regenerate_batch.go internal/engine/regenerate_write.go
result: line 786; res.Tag, res.Tag at regenerate_batch.go:361, req.Tag, req.Tag at regenerate_write.go:200

text: The provider release title stays the bare tag on the forward release and on both regenerate paths; the headline lives only in the body, where it renders as the first line under the title.
why: A headline-derived title would vary with whether the AI wrote one (the no-headline bodies, override repos and every release the doubt rule leaves without one would mix bare numbers with summaries), would make mint read into a body it passes through untouched, would retitle releases already out on regenerate, and gains only in the releases list; the bare tag also keeps regenerate --source tag's rebuild from the tag annotation body deterministic and parse-free.
rules_out: Lifting the headline into the provider release title
alternatives: B: lift the headline into the title where the body has one

text: Breaking changes get a 💥 Breaking section, first among the sections (after the headline where there is one); a breaking change is listed there only, not repeated in another section, and the section, like every section, is left out when empty.
why: A reader upgrading must meet what breaks before anything else.
evidence: Audit: breaking changes buried in 5 of 31
E1: 8 of 10 breaking bodies flagged against today's 1 of 10

text: A change is breaking where something users already do stops working, or gives a different result they must act on: a removed or renamed command, flag, option, setting or key binding; a default changed so existing setups behave differently in a way that matters; a changed output or file format that scripts or tools read; data or configuration from the previous release no longer read.
why: The narrow definition keeps the section from crying wolf at the top of the notes.

text: A change that only adds, keeps more, allows more or improves is not breaking, and when unsure a change is not breaking and goes in its usual section.
why: The section sits at the top of the notes, so a false alarm stands in the opening lines — the headline's own asymmetry: a missed flag costs what today's notes cost, a false one misstates the release where every reader looks. mint v0.0.2's new E1 notes opened on a false Breaking bullet.

text: Each Breaking bullet says in its one sentence what breaks and what to do, what to do coming only from what the diff shows (a new name, a replacement, a setting that keeps the old behaviour); where the diff shows none, the bullet says what breaks and stops there, never claiming outright that nothing replaces it.
why: An invented remedy is a false claim in the opening lines, and a diff-only view cannot show that something does not exist.

text: The sections keep one fixed order in every release whatever its main work — 💥 Breaking, ✨ Added, 🔧 Changed, ⚠️ Deprecated, 🗑️ Removed, 🐛 Fixed, 🔒 Security — with empty sections left out.
why: The headline already lifts the main work above every section, so reordering the sections would answer the same problem twice and cost readers an order they can rely on across versions.
rules_out: Notes that change shape from release to release
alternatives: Order by weight: the section holding the release's main work first

text: Every change is placed by comparing it with the previous release, never with earlier states inside this release.
why: The previous release is the only baseline a reader upgrading from it shares.

text: Added is something the previous release did not have, its pieces included even where the diff shows them adjusted, capped or fixed along the way: a bug in something new in this release is never Fixed, and a tweak to it is never Changed.
why: Placement is judged against the previous release.

text: Changed is a rework or redesign of something the previous release already had, and any smaller change to how it works that is not a fix (such as a speed-up users notice or a changed default that is not breaking); a genuinely new capability is Added, whether it ships inside a rework or is added to something the previous release had, such as a new option on an existing command.
why: Placement is judged against the previous release.

text: Fixed is something that behaved wrongly in the previous release (wrong output or placement, a crash or error, dropped or lost data, something not working) and now behaves correctly, however the diff or its comments frame it — including a rework whose purpose is the fix, and something an earlier release lost that this one brings back.
why: E1's behaviour-based definition of Fixed took Changed→Fixed misfiling from 23 to 14.

text: Removed is something the previous release had that is gone; a removal that breaks existing use goes under Breaking only.
why: A breaking change is listed in the Breaking section only.

text: Every change is listed once, in one section; the only restatement in the body is the headline's summary of the main work.

why: The answer is about the repo, not this release, and unwinding it would bring the same question back next time; the artifact commit sits beneath the answers commit, so the answers are re-committed after the reset.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: The unwind's narration names the answers commit as kept, so the commit left at the top of the branch does not read as an unwind that failed.
why: The unwind line is the operator's account of what mint undid; a line that hides the kept commit invites the reset that undoes it, bringing the same questions back.
rules_out: No mention of the kept commit
Narrating the commit only when it is made

cites.section: Narrating the Kept Answers Commit > Decision
Narrating the Kept Answers Commit > Options Considered

text: A failure writing `.mint.toml`, or staging or committing it, is a failure before the push: surfaced and routed through the unwind as a failed pre-tag artifact commit is, with the write error or git's own stderr verbatim beneath its line; the run aborts before any tag, the unwind leaves `.mint.toml` as it was before the answers were written, and nothing is recorded.
why: Every pre-push commit mint makes is surfaced and unwound on failure, and no answers commit exists to keep.

text: If the unwind's re-commit of the answers fails, one warning names the manual step that restores the answers, with git's own stderr verbatim beneath it; the narration then does not name the answers commit as kept, and the summary reports manual cleanup required rather than a clean repo.
why: Naming the commit kept when it is not would be the false claim the as-built unwind warning exists to prevent.

text: If the unwind's reset fails, no re-commit is attempted, since the answers commit is still on the branch; the as-built warning naming the reset as the manual step names after it the step that restores the answers, the narration does not name the answers commit as kept, and the summary reports manual cleanup required.
why: A re-commit on a branch the reset never moved would duplicate the commit or commit nothing, and the manual reset takes the answers with it.

text: When the answers leave no path in the diff, the release gets the maintenance-release body, as any empty post-exclusion diff does.
why: The as-built empty-diff body.

text: The commit-subject list leaves out subjects starting `chore(release): release-notes path answers for `, so the floor's `c`, `fallback` and a later regenerate's `c` never list mint's own answers commit.
why: The list is `git log --format=%s` over the range, so leaving the commit out means recognising its fixed subject; a tooling commit says nothing about what a release holds.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: Under `--autostash` the answers are written to the committed `.mint.toml`; a stashed edit to the same file that conflicts on restore leaves the stash entry intact, as any conflicting restore does.
why: mint never discards the operator's work.

text: When `.mint.toml` is untracked and a `.gitignore` rule matches it, the answers are written but not staged or committed; the recording line says they were written and not committed because git ignores the file, the release goes on, and an abort or failure after answering keeps the write. A tracked `.mint.toml` is committed whatever the ignore rules say.
why: Staging it would take `git add -f` and commit a config the operator keeps out of the repo; the answers then live on this machine, as the operator's config does, so this clone is not asked again.

text: What does the check do on an unattended run and on a dry run?
On an unattended run (`-y`, non-TTY, an agent run) there is no pause and nothing is written; a flagged file stays in the diff and is read like any other.
why: Fail loud, never hang; no file leaves the notes on the AI's say alone.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: On an unattended run each suggestion prints with its reason, what it matches as the pause would show it, and the `[release].diff_exclude` line that would exclude it: the key as an Exclude answer would leave it, holding its current entries with the suggested glob appended, or the glob alone where the key is unset, worked out against the config as loaded so it never carries another suggestion's glob.
why: For whoever reads the output to act on; a line holding the glob alone pasted beside an existing key would break the next strict load.

text: An unattended run's suggestions print whatever happens to the notes: after the notes when they are written, after the commit-subject list when `fallback` ships it, and with the floor's next moves when the run stops there.
why: A stopped run is where the reader acts, and a re-run repeats the same check and the same stop, so suggestions printed only after written notes would never reach that reader.
rules_out: Printing suggestions only after written notes

cites.section: Unattended Suggestions When the Notes Fail > Decision

text: On a dry run nothing is asked or written; the suggestions follow the dry run's own mode: at a terminal without `-y` they show as they would at the pause, and an unattended dry run prints them after the notes as an unattended run does, the `[release].diff_exclude` line included.
why: A dry run previews the real run it stands for; an agent previewing with `--dry-run -y` acts on the line the real run will print.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: What happens when the exclusion check itself fails?

The check counts as failed on a generation failure, a timeout, a missing binary, an answer mint cannot read, or a list that will not fit; in each case the release carries on with no suggestions, and any real AI problem surfaces at the notes call, which runs the same command through the normal failure path.
why: The check is advisory: it only proposes exclusions.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: A failed check prints one warning line, `couldn't check for files that don't belong in the notes`, with the AI's captured output verbatim beneath it where there is any, then carries on.
why: Otherwise "nothing looked out of place" and "the check never ran" look the same, which is how a design file slips into the notes unnoticed.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: The failure classifier never runs for the check itself, and a Ctrl-C during the check cancels the run.
why: The check's failure changes nothing that a classification could act on; a cancel propagates unchanged.

cites.section: Exclusion Suggestions Before the Notes > Decision

text: Where does a release's notes body come from, and in what order does the AI path run its steps?

The first match wins: `--notes-file` (the supplied body, no AI, no check, no cap); a first release (`Initial release.`, as built); an empty post-exclusion diff (the maintenance-release body, as built); `--no-ai` (the commit-subject list); then the AI path.
why: A supplied body needs none of the honest stand-in bodies the guards produce when there is nothing to summarise.

text: The AI path runs in order: the exclusion check (forward releases only; if its exclusions leave the diff empty the maintenance body applies); cache reuse after a dry run, as built; the size check of the composed single-pass prompt (instructions, Change Map condensed if over its share, diff, reminder) against `max_prompt_bytes`; under the cap one single-pass call, whose failure the classifier routes (SIZE halves, anything else to the floor); over the cap chunked generation, the single call skipped.
why: Exclusions change the diff the later steps see, so the size check measures what they leave.

text: A release over the cap only because of a file the operator excludes at the pause, such as a committed 1.9 MB transcript, is measured under the cap and gets an ordinary single-pass call.
why: The size check runs after the exclusion check, on the diff the exclusions leave.

text: Regenerate's fresh source follows the same path without the exclusion check and cache reuse, per version under `--all`: as built it neither offers notes from the dry-run cache nor writes to it.
why: The cache carries a release's dry-run preview to the real run that follows, and a regenerate is asked for new notes on a version already out.

text: What shape should a chunked release's stitch take: map-reduce, refine, or concatenation?
Parallel first: as much as possible runs in parallel, and never a chain of three or four serial AI requests.
why: The user's steer in research (2026-06-26): "the more we can do in parallel, the better".

text: The chunked path is map-reduce: chunk calls run in parallel, then exactly one merge call produces the final notes, the one serial step; refine is out, and concatenating the chunk notes is neither the plan nor a fallback.
why: Refine is serial by construction and biased toward early chunks; naive concatenation breaks salience and dedup.
rules_out: Refine: sequential calls each given the notes so far
Concatenation of partials as the plan

text: The degradation ladder is: a single-pass call, then map-reduce chunking (with halving after a SIZE answer), then the remediation floor as the last rung, never the plan; there is no concatenation rung.
why: Each rung is reached reactively when the one before cannot produce notes; a glued body ships a visibly broken result worst when nobody reviews.

cites.section: Thread: the degradation ladder — resolving reduce-step failure (F1, F7) (2026-06-26)

text: The Change Map is cheap and bounded by file count rather than diff size: two git calls (`--name-status`, `--numstat`) rendered as structural novelty, churn by area and notable files; it is not strictly size-independent, since it lists renames and removals one line per path.
how: Read from `internal/notes/changemap.go`.

cites.section: Stitching and Salience: the Change Map as Spine > Journey

text: Every chunk call and the merge call receive the same whole-release Change Map.
why: Each chunk then knows the whole release's shape while reading only its slice, and the merge can rank across all of it; the default prompt's salience rules rank by the map.

cites.section: 8.2 The Change Map in every call
Stitching and Salience: the Change Map as Spine > Decision

text: When the Change Map would take more than its share of the cap, its long runs of removed or renamed files condense by folder (e.g. `Removed: 4,312 files under vendor/`), in every call that carries the map, single-pass included; a map that fits renders exactly as today.
why: A release deleting a vendored tree or moving thousands of files would otherwise crowd out any diff; the notes still learn the tree went, which is all they would say about it.
rules_out: Stopping at the floor with a `diff_exclude` hint

cites.section: 8.2 The Change Map in every call

text: How are a release's files packed into chunk calls, and what happens to a single file too big for one call?

cites.section: Chunk Boundaries and the Single-File Floor > Context

text: A chunk call's room for diff is the cap minus its fixed part (instructions, Change Map, chunk framing, reminder); files are packed in path order, each chunk filled until the next file's diff would not fit in its room.
why: Path order keeps each area's files together (the Change Map's area is a path's leading directory), and each folder's, with no grouping step, so a feature is seen whole by one call.
rules_out: A serial ask-the-AI-to-group round-trip

cites.section: Chunk Boundaries and the Single-File Floor > Decision

text: A file whose diff alone exceeds a chunk call's room is split into pieces, each a chunk call of its own sent in parallel and stitched by the merge like any other chunk notes; nothing in the diff is dropped or stood in for.
why: Whether a big file is hand-written or generated cannot be judged reliably and depends on the project, and the exclusion check has already settled whether each file belongs, so a file still in the diff is wanted and is read.
rules_out: A one-line stand-in for the file
An AI verdict of hand-written versus generated deciding stand-in or pieces
Truncating the file to fit

cites.section: 8.4 A file too big for one call: pieces
Chunk Boundaries and the Single-File Floor > Decision > 2026-10-17 — revised

text: Pieces are cut at hunk boundaries, else line boundaries, and a single line longer than the room (a minified bundle) at a character boundary; each piece carries the file's diff header and says which piece of how many it is.
why: Nothing is dropped and no character is split, and the call reading a piece knows which file it holds.

cites.section: 8.4 A file too big for one call: pieces

text: How many chunk calls run at once?

cites.section: Thread: review-003 — parallelism on a sequential codebase (F1/F2/F3, one root) (2026-07-01)

text: At most four chunk calls run at once, a fixed bound, not a setting.
why: Unbounded fan-out would put the whole wave on the machine and on the provider's rate and usage limits at once; four keeps most of the parallel speed for the 3–20-chunk releases research expected.

cites.section: When the Whole Wave Fails > Decision

text: What does each chunk and merge call carry, and what happens to a call that cannot be made under the cap?

A chunk call carries the release's instructions (the default prompt with `context`, or the `[release].prompt` override, which replaces both, as built), the Change Map, framing naming its part (part k of n; for a piece, the file and which piece of how many), its slice and the closing reminder, and returns notes for its part in the release's notes format.
why: The release's instructions define the notes' format and rules for every call; mint adds only the framing that says which part a call holds.

text: The merge call carries the release's instructions, the Change Map, every chunk's notes in chunk order, framing asking for one set of release notes that combines related changes across parts, drops duplicates and ranks by the Change Map, and the closing reminder; its output is the notes body, passed through byte-identical like a single-pass body.
why: The merge is where cross-chunk salience is restored.

text: mint's framing is fixed text of its own; its exact wording is the implementer's.
why: The specification fixes only what the framing must say.

text: When a call's fixed part leaves no room for diff even with the Change Map condensed, from an outsized `[release].prompt` or `context` (operator text mint never trims), a `max_prompt_bytes` below the fixed part of mint's own instructions with neither key set, or a halving round aimed below the fixed part, mint sends no call and the run falls to the floor with guidance naming which it was.
why: No call ever exceeds the cap, and condensing is the only shrink mint makes to its own fixed part.

cites.section: Stitching and Salience: the Change Map as Spine > Decision

text: A merge prompt that would exceed the cap is not sent, and counts as a failed merge.
why: The merge's input overflows only with hundreds of chunks; were it over the cap, no merge call could be made.

text: Chunk notes are held in memory for the run, and persist only in a failure's saved file and in the dry-run cache.
why: No resume state is kept beyond those two.

text: Should there be a setting deciding how a too-big release is handled (break it up versus not), and should chunking ask for consent to its extra calls?

cites.section: Thread: config knob for oversize handling (2026-06-26)

text: Chunking has no setting: there is no `oversize` key and no way to switch it off; `max_prompt_bytes` stays the only size setting.
why: Chunking only happens when a release cannot go in one call, so switching it off would only mean such releases get no AI notes, which nobody wants as a standing policy, and `--no-ai` and `--notes-file` already cover a release that should not get AI notes; a key is cheap to add and costly to remove under strict config, so one can be added if a real case appears, such as an API-key setup where the extra calls cost money.
rules_out: An `oversize = chunk | off` key
A `chunk` value on `on_notes_failure`

text: Chunking needs no consent prompt for its extra calls: it handles the release without asking ("it just handles it").
why: The user's call in research to auto-degrade silently by default; "silent" means no consent prompt, not no narration.

cites.section: Thread: config knob for oversize handling (2026-06-26)

text: What should trigger degradation once a notes call fails: string-matching the provider's overflow message, splitting on any failure, or asking the AI to classify its own error?

cites.section: Thread: AI-as-error-classifier — "ask the AI what its own error means" (user proposal, 2026-06-29) [STRONG]

text: The transport's failure causes: `ErrGenerationFailed` (a non-zero exit or empty body surviving one retry, overloaded across size, auth, rate limits, refusals and network blips), `ErrTimeout` (per-attempt deadline, not retried), `ErrCommandMissing` (no binary), and `context.Canceled` (propagated unchanged); there is no structured "too long" classification.
how: Read from `internal/ai/transport.go`.

cites.section: Thread: the chunking trigger — proactive vs reactive (F5, F8), researched from transport code (2026-06-26)

text: When a release-notes generation call (single-pass, chunk or merge) fails, mint asks the same AI what its own error means through the existing transport and `ai_command`, with no new AI seam, and only a size answer starts the degradation ladder; this reactive classify-on-failure is the primary trigger.
why: It is provider-agnostic by construction, and it never fires a wave of calls at a failure chunking cannot fix (a rate limit, a server error, an expired login). Accepted cost: one extra AI call per failure.
rules_out: String-matching the provider's overflow message
Split-and-observe: breaking the release up on any failure

text: The classifier runs only on a generation failure (a non-zero exit, or an empty body, surviving the transport's single retry); timeouts, missing binaries and cancels are told apart by the transport and never reach it.
why: Only there does mint know the binary ran and said something.

text: A missing binary falls to the floor.
why: Splitting cannot fix it.

text: A cancel (`context.Canceled`) propagates unchanged and never falls to `on_notes_failure`.
why: A cancel is not an AI failure.

text: The classifier is release-notes only, for forward release and regenerate: `mint commit` makes no classify call, and the exclusion check never classifies its own failures.
why: The classifier's only distinct reaction is the ladder, which commit lacks; every commit failure already ends in the editor, so a classify call would only delay it by one call.

text: Should a timed-out notes call start the degradation ladder, and how does the per-attempt timeout read across a wave of calls?
A timeout never starts the ladder; it falls to the floor. The rule is revisited if timeouts show up on releases that sit under any sensible cap.
why: A timeout is not evidence of size, and a wave fired at a slow service multiplies the wait; the cap absorbs "too slow because too big" before any call is sent.
rules_out: Chunking on a timed-out single-pass call

text: The per-attempt timeout applies to each call on its own, every chunk call, the merge and the classify call, with no overall deadline across the calls; a wave takes roughly its rounds of chunk calls plus the merge, and a chunk call's timeout is a final failure that ends the wave.
why: An overall deadline would be a second timing rule whose right value grows with the release, exactly what the per-call cap exists to avoid predicting.

text: What does the classify prompt carry, and how is the untrusted error text embedded in it?

The classify call goes through the existing transport with the release's `ai_command` and timeout; its prompt carries the two codes, each with a one-line gloss (SIZE for a request too large for the model's context window or input limit, OTHER for anything else), the failed call's captured stdout and stderr, both streams, fenced as captured tool output and explicitly not instructions, and an instruction to answer with exactly one code.
why: The error text is the AI command's own output, which mint does not control; standard untrusted-content hygiene. Both streams, because tools write errors to either. The stakes are bounded: the answer only picks a branch, and under the lean command the call has no tools to act through.

text: Each captured stream longer than 4,000 bytes keeps its first and last 2,000 bytes, cut at character boundaries, with a line saying how many bytes were omitted between them.
why: Causes sit at either end of a failure's output (claude's overflow message, a Go panic at the top, a Python traceback at the bottom), and a few kilobytes keeps the call small.

cites.section: Classifier Bound and Answer Reading > Decision

text: Under a cap smaller than the classify prompt, the classify call is not sent, and the failure takes the OTHER path, as when the classify call fails.
why: No call mint makes is ever bigger than the cap.

text: Which codes should the classifier's closed set hold: minimal SIZE / OTHER, or a rich per-cause set?

cites.section: Closed Code Set: Minimal vs Rich Granularity > Context
Thread: the classifier's closed code-set — what it must cover (2026-06-29)

text: The classifier ships SIZE and OTHER only.
why: Only about three reactions exist however many codes are defined (split, retry or back off, surface and stop), and no code beyond SIZE has a reaction worth its cost for the subscription case: TRANSIENT has had the transport's retry, AUTH/QUOTA/REFUSAL all stop, and the AI's verbatim message is more specific than mint's wording.
rules_out: A rich set: SIZE / RATE_LIMIT / AUTH / TRANSIENT / QUOTA / REFUSAL / OTHER

cites.section: Closed Code Set: Minimal vs Rich Granularity > Decision
Closed Code Set: Minimal vs Rich Granularity > Options Considered

text: SIZE fires the ladder: halving for a single-pass or chunk call; on the merge call, a failed merge.
why: Size is the only failure chunking can fix.

text: OTHER means no split: the run falls to the floor, ending the degradation, not the run's notes policy; on release `on_notes_failure` then applies exactly as today.
why: OTHER stops degrading; the exemption of only a cancel from `on_notes_failure` reads as an exception only if the OTHER path falls to it.

cites.section: Closed Code Set: Minimal vs Rich Granularity > Decision

text: The code set extends additively: a RATE_LIMIT code, with a wait-and-retry that would be a deliberate exception to "consumers never re-retry", can be added if API-key setups hit throttling mid-wave; anything unrecognised already falls to OTHER.
why: On a subscription a usage limit is a window of hours a CLI run should not sit out; on an API key a 429 clears in seconds, but the case has not been observed.

cites.section: Closed Code Set: Minimal vs Rich Granularity > Journey

text: How is the classifier's answer read, and what if it is not one listed code?

cites.section: Classifier Bound and Answer Reading > Context

text: mint strips surrounding whitespace, quotes, backticks and trailing punctuation from the answer and compares the rest case-insensitively; it is a listed code only when exactly `SIZE` or exactly `OTHER`, and anything else (a sentence, both codes, an unknown word) maps to OTHER.
why: A model told to answer with one code still sometimes adds a full stop, a quote or a capital; mapping a decorated `SIZE.` to OTHER would stop a release chunking could have saved.

cites.section: Classifier Bound and Answer Reading > Decision

text: There is no firmer re-ask: an answer that is not exactly one listed code maps straight to OTHER. Worst case, the error surfaces where chunking might have helped.
why: The transport owns validation and the single retry, and consumers never re-retry; the OTHER catch-all already guarantees safe termination.

text: What happens when there is no error text, when the classify call itself fails or is cancelled, and should the transport's retry fire before the classifier?

cites.section: Transport Retry Before the Classifier > Context

text: When both captured streams are empty or whitespace-only, mint skips the classify call and takes the OTHER path directly.
why: Classifying nothing could only be a guess, and a guessed SIZE would fire the whole wave at a failure chunking cannot fix.

text: A generation failure, timeout or missing binary on the classify call takes the OTHER path, and the output rendered is still the original call's, never the classify call's.
why: When the tool's overhead alone overflows the window the classify call fails the same way, which is the correct stop: splitting cannot fix it.

text: A cancel during the classify call propagates unchanged and never falls to `on_notes_failure`.
why: A cancel is not an AI failure.

text: The transport's single retry stays, for every call including the classify call, so an under-cap overflow sends the identical call twice before the classifier looks. Revisited if under-cap overflows become routine, for example on smaller-window models run with the cap left at the default.
why: On claude the repeated overflow costs one more round trip, a second or two with no tokens charged, and the cap makes under-cap overflows rare, so making the retry rule depend on the calling command is not worth the saving.
rules_out: Classifying before any retry, so SIZE chunks with no repeat

cites.section: Transport Retry Before the Classifier > Decision > 2026-10-18 — revised
Transport Retry Before the Classifier > Options Considered

text: Does the classifier's result replace the AI's raw error output or sit alongside it?

cites.section: Classifier Result Alongside the Verbatim Error > Context

text: The classifier adds to the AI's verbatim output and never replaces it: its code drives control flow (split or stop) and selects the ✗ line's cause phrase and mint's guidance, while the AI's captured output still renders verbatim beneath the ✗ line.
why: Subprocess failure diagnostics travel verbatim, never reworded, and the AI's own text is often the most specific remediation, such as `Not logged in · Please run /login` or claude's token breakdown.

cites.section: Classifier Result Alongside the Verbatim Error > Decision

text: What can mint do when an explicit `ai_command`'s own overhead alone overflows the window?
Chunking shrinks only mint's own prompt, and every chunk re-pays the AI tool's overhead, so chunking cannot save a failure where the overhead alone nears the window.
how: Reasoned in research from the live agentic-workflows failure.

cites.section: Thread: LIVE real-world overflow — agentic-workflows v0.5.12 (2026-07-01) [EMPIRICAL, refines F1/F2]

text: A repo whose own `ai_command` carries an overhead that alone overflows the window takes the OTHER path: its classify call fails the same way, so no split, the AI's verbatim message, then the floor; mint's guidance points at the documented lean command rather than naming claude flags itself.
why: The lean default removes the case for the shipped command; for explicit commands mint can only advise, and keeping claude's flags in the documentation keeps per-provider knowledge out of mint's code.

cites.section: 9.7 An explicit `ai_command` that carries its own overhead

text: What happens when a call already under the cap comes back SIZE?

On a SIZE answer for a diff-carrying call (the single-pass call or a chunk call), mint halves: the new target is half the composed size of the call that failed (instructions, Change Map, framing, diff and reminder), and the slice it carried is re-cut at that target by the first wave's packing and piece rules, so a single-pass call that fails SIZE becomes a chunked run at half its size.
why: It still produces notes without mint knowing the window, and its cost lands where the misconfiguration is.
rules_out: Treating an under-cap overflow as misconfiguration and stopping

cites.section: Halving Bound and the Lower-the-Cap Hint > Decision

text: Each call in a halved round has its own room for diff, whatever its fixed part leaves; a round aimed below the fixed part has no room, and no call is sent.
why: The cap bounds whole composed calls.

cites.section: Halving Bound and the Lower-the-Cap Hint > Journey

text: A SIZE answer on the merge call is not halved; it is a failed merge.
why: Halving a merge would be the recursive-collapse reduce that is ruled out by the no-serial-depth steer.
rules_out: A recursive-collapse reduce

text: A slice is halved at most three times, counted from its first SIZE answer, taking it to an eighth of the size that first failed; a fourth SIZE fails that slice, and a failed slice fails the generation.
why: A cap wrong for its model by more than eight times is not a slight miscalibration.

cites.section: Halving Bound and the Lower-the-Cap Hint > Decision

text: Halving's rounds are serial, a deliberate exception to the parallel-first shape.
why: The path is rare when the cap fits the model, and its cost lands where the misconfiguration is.

text: When the notes were written after halving, mint says after the notes that the cap is set higher than this model accepts, and suggests the size of the largest call that succeeded in the run.
why: It turns a quiet absorption into something the operator can fix; the largest successful call is one the model demonstrably accepted.

cites.section: Halving Bound and the Lower-the-Cap Hint > Decision

text: The hint's suggestion is that call's exact size in bytes, written as the value to set (e.g. `max_prompt_bytes = 1260000`), never rounded.
why: A size rounded up would sit above the largest call the model accepted.

text: Only diff-carrying calls count toward the hint's size: the single-pass, chunk and piece calls, not the merge, classify or exclusion-check calls.
why: Those are the calls that overflowed and that the cap sizes; a merge carries notes prose of no measured density.

text: Under `regenerate --all` the hint prints once, at the end of the batch, naming the largest such call that succeeded across the batch, however the batch ends once any version's notes were written after halving, a declined gate, a failed `r` or a Ctrl-C included; it records no state, so printing it on the way out leaves a cancel clean.
why: The batch runs under one cap and one command, so per-version hints would repeat one remedy with sizes to reconcile.

text: When halving runs out, the floor's guidance names both causes: the model accepts less than the cap (lower `max_prompt_bytes`), or the command carries a large overhead of its own (use the documented lean command).
why: mint cannot tell a small window from a large command overhead: in both, even small pieces come back SIZE while the small classify call fits.

text: When one chunk of a parallel wave fails, does the whole generation fail, or does the merge proceed with the surviving chunks?

cites.section: Thread: closing the first review — cancellation (F6) & quality bar (F4) (2026-06-29)

text: One failed chunk fails the generation: a chunk or piece ends in failure after its transport retry, its classify call and, on SIZE, its halving rounds, or on a timeout or missing binary; then no merge runs, mint saves the notes of the chunks that did finish and names the file, and the run goes to the floor.
why: The missing slice can be the release's headline feature; notes that read as complete while quietly leaving out the biggest change are the very failure the feature exists to end, and under `-y` they would ship unreviewed.
rules_out: Merging what came back and flagging the missing slice

cites.section: 11.1 One failed chunk fails the generation

text: On single-pass notes `r` re-runs the AI path from the size check onward with the nudge appended, so the cap, the classifier and halving apply as to the first attempt (a nudge pushing the prompt over the cap sends the release to chunking); it never re-runs the exclusion check.
why: Its call is a release-notes generation call like any other; the check asks about paths, not notes, and its answers were recorded before the first attempt.

text: The nudge rides in the release's instructions, so when the ladder turns an `r` into a chunked run, every chunk, piece and halving-round call and the merge carry it.
why: As built the nudge is appended to the instructions, which ride in every call.

text: A failed `r` aborts the run whatever `on_notes_failure` says, as built; on a release the abort unwinds back to the starting commit, taking the pre-tag artifact commit with it, and an `r` ending because stdin closed at its nudge prompt counts as a failed `r`.
why: As built a failed `r` aborts; every pre-push mutation is unwound on failure.

text: On chunked notes, or a single-pass `r` the ladder turned chunked, a failed `r` first saves the per-chunk notes and names the file with `mint release --notes-file <path>`; `on_notes_failure` does not apply, so `fallback` never ships its body in place of the re-merge asked for, and the abort lands before any tag.
why: The saved notes can still go out through `--notes-file`.

text: A Ctrl-C during an `r`, the merge-only `r`'s re-merge call included, is a cancel, not a failed `r`, and saves no chunk notes.
why: A cancel is not an AI failure, and a Ctrl-C mid-wave saves none.

text: Every way the review gate ends a release before the push, a decline (as built), a failed `r`, a launched editor failing at the gate's `e`, or stdin closing at its keypress, unwinds back to the starting commit, taking the pre-tag artifact commit with it; a missing editor still warns and returns to the gate; regenerate's review gate lands before its changelog commit, so an abort there has nothing to reset.
why: Every pre-push mutation is tracked and unwound on failure, and the gate sits after the pre-tag artifact commit.

text: At a single-version regenerate's review gate, `r` works as at a release's: merge-only on chunked notes, the AI path from the size check on single-pass notes; a failed `r` aborts the regenerate, first saving the per-chunk notes where chunked, which go onto the version with `mint release regenerate <version> --notes-file <path>`.
why: The merge decides emphasis and ordering whichever verb runs the gate; re-running the wave would cost the minutes and usage-window draw `r` set out to avoid.

text: At each of `regenerate --all`'s per-version review gates (at a terminal without `-y`), `r` follows the same rules; a failed `r` saves that version's per-chunk notes where chunked, names the file with that version's `mint release regenerate <version> --notes-file <path>`, and ends the batch, as a failed gate does as built; it is not the batch's floor, so the batch does not skip the version and carry on.
why: A failed `r` aborts whatever `on_notes_failure` says, so it is not the floor; treating it as a skip would make it a floor on one verb only.
rules_out: A failed `r` skipping the version and continuing the batch

text: The notes cache keys on inputs, not output: `notescache.Key(diff, version, instructions)` hashes the post-exclusion diff, the version and the resolved instructions.

text: A dry run's chunked notes are cached and offered back to the real run exactly like single-pass notes, sparing the real run the whole wave.
why: The cache keys on inputs, so non-deterministic chunked output does not cause a miss.

text: A chunked body is cached together with its per-chunk notes, so `r` on reused chunked notes re-runs only the merge.
why: Storing only the final body would make `r` on reused notes re-run the whole wave, the cost merge-only `r` set out to avoid.

text: The per-chunk notes share the cache entry's lifecycle and need no cleanup of their own: the entry is outside the repo, pruned to the latest per project on every write, stale after the ~1h TTL, and keyed on the version so it cannot match once the release is tagged.
why: As-built cache properties.

cites.section: Scope Across the Three Consumers > Decision

text: The cache is written on real runs as well as dry runs, as built, and an entry holds the per-chunk notes whichever run wrote it, so a real run aborted at the review gate leaves chunked notes the next run can reuse; outside the cache entry the per-chunk notes live only in memory, and only a failure's saved file persists.
why: The cache keys on inputs, not on which run wrote it.

text: A chunked run keeps the single notes line and updates it as the run moves, in the agreed mock's words: `Checking for files that don't belong in the notes…`, `Writing notes: {size} release, in {n} parts · {k} of {n} done`, `Writing notes: part {k} was too big for the model, retrying it as {n} smaller parts`, `Writing notes: merging {n} parts`, then `✓ Notes written ({n} parts, merged) ({elapsed})`.
why: A spinner sitting minutes looks the same whether mint is working or hung; one updated line shows the run is alive and roughly how far along, without adding lines.

text: A single-pass call that halves shows `Writing notes: too big for the model in one call, retrying in {n} parts`; here and when a part halves, n is the number of parts the re-cut yields, three or more; the run is then a chunked run, so the line moves to the split line with the same composed single-pass size, and plain mode prints one line per finished part.
why: Every smaller call still carries the whole fixed part, so each has room for less than half the failed call's diff and a re-cut always yields three parts or more.

why: One total serves both places in the line, rather than the done count running past it.

text: Should `mint commit`'s AI-failure path carry the AI's captured output, which it drops as built?
Attended, `mint commit`'s AI-failure warning, `could not generate a message, opening editor`, carries the AI's captured output verbatim beneath it, then the editor opens as built.
why: Subprocess failure diagnostics travel verbatim; it matters for an expired login, a usage limit, or a claude too old for the lean flags.

text: Unattended (`-y` or non-TTY), when `mint commit` fails loud because the AI failed, the failure carries the AI's captured output verbatim beneath its `no AI message and no interactive editor available` line.
why: The unattended run is the one with nobody present to re-run it, so it needs the cause most.

text: The other triggers into commit's editor fallback, `--no-ai`, an oversized prompt and an all-excluded diff, carry no AI output, and their lines are unchanged.
why: There is no AI output to carry.
